 A MARTÍNEZ, HOST: Every December, the Kennedy Center Honors puts a spotlight on major stars in the performing arts. With the center's main theater still closed, this year's event will be held at the Capital One Arena in Washington, D.C. Now, that's not the only change. The arts complex is preparing to switch its ticketing operations to the behemoth Ticketmaster. An NPR investigation has found that move raises ethical concerns. NPR culture correspondent Anastasia Tsioulcas has been looking into this. So, Anastasia, the big event is coming soon with lots of changes. What are some of the changes? ANASTASIA TSIOULCAS, BYLINE: Well, it is less than a month from the honors ceremony. But it's still unclear how or when people can actually get tickets. So, A, current and former staffers have told me the delay's due to the Kennedy Center's decision to swap ticketing platforms for Ticketmaster. And these staffers have asked for anonymity for fear of repercussion and their ability to continue to work in arts administration. MARTÍNEZ: So we know that when President Trump became the Kennedy Center's board chairman shortly after taking office, there were leadership changes at the center. So who was leading this drive to make that switch over to Ticketmaster? TSIOULCAS: That's unclear. What we have learned, though, is that while the new partnership with Ticketmaster was being negotiated, the president of the Kennedy Center was Richard Grenell. So a few months after Grenell arrived at the Kennedy Center, he was also appointed to the board of Live Nation, which is Ticketmaster's parent company. And according to Live Nation's SEC filings, Grenell was paid over $260,000 as one of its board members. Plus, he was given a small amount of Live Nation stock. Now, Grenell's since left his position at the Kennedy Center. We reached out to him, but he did not respond. MARTÍNEZ: All right. So he held those two positions at the same time. I mean, it sounds like it could be a conflict of interest. TSIOULCAS: Well, that's what ethics experts are saying. I recently spoke to Richard Briffault. He's a professor at Columbia Law School who specializes in government ethics. Let's take a listen. RICHARD BRIFFAULT: If you sit on the board and, at the same time, you have a financial stake in another entity that does business with and benefits from the business with the entity on whose board you sit, that's a problem. TSIOULCAS: Essentially, he's saying you can't represent both sides of a deal. MARTÍNEZ: OK. Now, what does the Kennedy Center have to say? TSIOULCAS: Both the Kennedy Center and Ticketmaster are saying they began discussions in early 2024, and Ticketmaster said Kennedy Center team members approached them wanting to switch. However, other current and former Kennedy Center staff who also asked for anonymity due to fears of retaliation have told us that time frame is not correct. In a message to NPR, a former senior executive wrote, quote, "I was against having Ticketmaster at the Kennedy Center," and they say the organization already had a system in place that worked. MARTÍNEZ: Anastasia, I'm on the website right now. I'm looking at it. If I wanted to go, I don't see a way for me to even try to go. So what happens now? TSIOULCAS: Yeah. And I'm watching, too, to see how and when people can get tickets to the Kennedy Center Honors. And, A, with a new Democratic-majority Congress coming into power, we'll see if there are any new investigations. MARTÍNEZ: All right. That's NPR's Anastasia Tsioulcas. Thanks a lot. TSIOULCAS: Thanks for having me. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
